newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya coffee blossoms despite lack of rain.
newsitem.headline: Kenya coffee blossoms despite lack of rain.

text.p: Coffee trees are blossoming in the lush hightop farmlands of central Kenya despite poor rains, and stable output is forecast for 1996/97.
A senior Coffee Board of Kenya official told Reuters that production estimates for 1996/97 had been scaled down to around 96,000 tonnes from previous forecasts of 100,000.
But production would still be in line with the results of previous years -- 94,800 tonnes in 1994/95 and 95,000 in 1995/96, according to Coffee Board of Kenya figures.

Higher world prices have inspired better crop husbandry, and growers see their prospects as being much brighter than at any other time this decade, farmers and officials from the major farm agencies told Reuters.

"The rains don't seem to be in our favour. We are watching the skies and praying," smallholder Njenga Kinuthia said. "But we haven't hit the lowest (rain) levels yet and with better money we have tended our crop better."
Coffee trees carpet Kinuthia's one hectare of land near Murang'a, 80 km north of Nairobi.
With Kenyan authorities easing restrictions on intercropping, Kinuthia has also planted peas and some tubers.

"That (intercropping) enhances farm incomes and food security," said Kinuthia. "It is also good that uprooting coffee will no longer be a criminal offence, you put your effort into the crop and if you fail you change -- very satisfying."
Kinuthia is one of the 300,000 smallholders who produce an estimated 65 percent of Kenya's total output.
John Kyendo, another smallholder, said the main problems remained credit and infrastructure, although higher world prices meant that many farmers could buy fertiliser.

"You could say that inputs use is low because of low or lack of credit. But with better (world) prices, at least more farmers are buying the fertilisers and sprays. That explains the stable or better crop expected all round," Kyendo told Reuters.
Kyendo said farmers lacked proper advice from agriculture extention officers who simply never turned up on farms.
He added that some cooperatives stores were too congested, which affected the moisture content of the coffee beans.

"Farmers need to be told how to produce the best from their tiny patches of land," Kyendo said, adding that poor roads meant it took time to reach markets and that a lack of services such as tap water and electricity meant farmers were not satisfied that the government used their earnings to improve their villages.
